```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", out.width = "100%", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5)
# The article downloads its readings from the Prometheus servers of the live app while it is
# built. They are downloaded here first, out of sight, to check that the servers answer with
# what the chunks below need: without it the code is shown without its results instead of
# failing the build. The chunks download the readings again, which takes a second or two.
online <- tryCatch(
  local({
    enviro_plus <- "http://pip1.crabdance.com:1507/api/v1/query_range"
    a_year_ago <- format(Sys.time() - 365 * 24 * 60 * 60, "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ", tz = "UTC")
    week <- golemenviro::get_data(urlq = enviro_plus)
    year <- golemenviro::get_data(start_time = a_year_ago, urlq = enviro_plus)
    enviro <- golemenviro::get_data(urlq = "http://pip1.crabdance.com:1505/api/v1/query_range")
    all(c("Temperature", "Humidity", "Pressure", "Reducing", "PM2.5") %in% names(week)) &&
      "PM2.5" %in% names(year) && "Temperature" %in% names(enviro)
  }),
  error = function(e) FALSE
)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = online)
```

`r if (!online) "> The readings could not be downloaded when this page was built, so the code is shown without its results."`

The charts of the [golemenviro app](https://sedzinfo-golemenviro.share.connect.posit.cloud/) are also R functions. Each one takes readings downloaded from a Prometheus server and returns an interactive [plotly](https://plotly.com/r/) chart. Run it in the console and the chart opens in the RStudio Viewer or your browser. In an R Markdown or Quarto document it appears in the page.

This article shows the gauges of the Current tab and the chart of the Time Series tab. [Daily pattern and comfort](daily-pattern.html) shows the charts of the hourly averages, and [Air quality](air-quality.html) the daily averages of the particles against the guidelines of the World Health Organization.

## Install and load the package

```{r install, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("golemenviro",
  repos = c("https://sedzinfo.r-universe.dev", "https://cloud.r-project.org"))
```

```{r library}
library(golemenviro)
```

## The servers

Each device runs [enviroplus_exporter](https://github.com/tijmenvandenbrink/enviroplus_exporter), which reads its sensors, and a Prometheus server, which collects and keeps the readings. The functions take the `query_range` address of that server. The two servers of the live app need no API key or password:

```{r servers}
prometheus_url <- c(
  "http://pip1.crabdance.com:1507/api/v1/query_range",
  "http://pip1.crabdance.com:1505/api/v1/query_range"
)
```

The first device has all the sensors of an Enviro+. The second, like an Enviro, has no gas or particle sensors. The [README](https://github.com/sedzinfo/golemenviro#readme) shows how to set up a device of your own.

## Time zone

The functions show the times in the time zone of your R session, which `app_time_zone()` returns. The app shows them in the time zone given to `pimoroni()`, `"Europe/Bucharest"` by default. To see the same times as the app, set it at the start of the session:

```{r timezone}
Sys.setenv(TZ = "Europe/Bucharest")
app_time_zone()
```

## Download the readings

`get_data()` downloads the readings of all the sensors of one server, by default over the last 7 days:

```{r data}
week <- get_data(urlq = prometheus_url[1])
names(week)
tail(week[, c("Date", "Temperature", "Humidity", "Pressure", "PM2.5")], 3)
```

It returns about 1,000 rows: over 7 days, a reading every 10 minutes. `Date` is the time of the reading and `Timestamp` the same time in seconds, followed by a column per sensor.

Sensors whose readings never change are left out, as the device does not have them. The second server has no columns for the gases and the particles:

```{r enviro}
names(get_data(urlq = prometheus_url[2]))
```

When a server cannot be reached, or sends no data, `get_data()` returns `NULL` with a message.

## Gauges

`plot_gauge()` draws the last reading of one sensor as a gauge, as the Current tab does. `variable` is the name of its column:

```{r gauge-temperature, fig.height = 4}
plot_gauge(week, "Temperature")
```

The big number is the last reading, and the small one under it its difference from the reference point, the thin line across the gauge. The green band is a comfortable or recommended range: 20 to 25 °C, 40 to 60% humidity, 1,010 to 1,015 hPa and 1,000 to 1,500 lux.

For PM2.5 and PM10 the green band reaches up to the guideline of the World Health Organization for the average of a day. PM1, which has none, gets that of PM2.5. A note under the gauges of the particles and the gases says what they measure:

```{r gauge-pm25, fig.height = 4}
plot_gauge(week, "PM2.5")
```

The gas and proximity sensors have no fixed scale, so their gauge is scaled to all the readings you pass: from the lowest to the highest, widened by one standard deviation. The green band is the mean plus or minus one standard deviation, and the reference point is the mean. The app passes the last 7 days, as here:

```{r gauge-reducing, fig.height = 4}
plot_gauge(week, "Reducing")
```

## Time series

`plot_time_series()` draws the readings of one sensor, as the Time Series tab does, with their moving average and their mean. On the right it sums them up: the last reading, the mean (μ), the minimum and maximum, the standard deviation (σ), the range, and the first and last day. `scale` is the title of the y axis:

```{r time-series}
plot_time_series(week, "Temperature", scale = degrees_celsius)
```

`degrees_celsius` and `micrograms_m3` hold the units with their special characters, as `symbol_mean` and `symbol_sd` hold μ and σ.

The moving average, Smoothing, is the mean of `k` readings centred on each one, 30 by default: about 5 hours over 7 days. A larger `k` smooths more.

For another period, pass its start, and its end if not now, with `start_time` and `end_time`. They are in UTC, written as `"2025-01-31T11:48:08Z"`. Whatever the period, `get_data()` returns about 1,000 readings, so a chart of a year is as light as one of a week:

```{r time-series-year}
a_year_ago <- Sys.time() - 365 * 24 * 60 * 60
start_time <- format(a_year_ago, "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ", tz = "UTC")
year <- get_data(start_time = start_time, urlq = prometheus_url[1])
plot_time_series(year, "PM2.5", scale = micrograms_m3)
```

From about 6 weeks on, the readings are an hour or more apart, and each is the average of the readings since the previous one, so short spikes are averaged away. Over a year each one covers almost 9 hours, and the moving average about 11 days.

## Save or change a chart

The charts are plotly objects, so the functions of the plotly and htmlwidgets packages work on them. To save a chart as a web page that opens in any browser:

```{r save, eval = FALSE}
chart <- plot_time_series(week, "Temperature", scale = degrees_celsius)
htmlwidgets::saveWidget(chart, "temperature.html")
```

To change the layout, for example the title:

```{r layout, eval = FALSE}
plotly::layout(chart, title = "Temperature over the last week")
```

## Run the app

`pimoroni()` starts the app with the servers you give it and opens it in your browser. Its `timezone` argument sets the time zone of the app:

```{r app, eval = FALSE}
pimoroni(prometheus_url = prometheus_url)
```
